lessons.title: Installing Front Fairing and Windscreen
lessons.body:
Start by laying out the front fairing, windscreen, and all mounting hardware on a clean cloth. Check the fairing for cracks or scratches, especially around the mounting holes. If any holes are cracked, reinforce them with a small piece of fibreglass mat and resin, then let it cure for at least 2 hours before installation. You will need a 10mm socket and ratchet, a Phillips screwdriver, and a torque wrench that reads up to 10 Nm. Most EV motorbike fairings use M6 bolts with rubber grommets to reduce vibration.

Position the fairing on the bike, aligning the top mounting tabs with the brackets on the steering head. Start all bolts by hand first to avoid cross-threading. Once all bolts are in, tighten them in a crisscross pattern to 8 Nm. Do not overtightenâplastic cracks easily. If the fairing uses quick-release fasteners, push them in until they click. For the windscreen, apply a thin bead of silicone sealant around the mounting edge to prevent rattles. Use M5 screws with plastic washers, and tighten to 3 Nm. If the windscreen is polycarbonate, clean it with a soft cloth and soapy water only; never use petrol or alcohol as it clouds the plastic.

In many African workshops, you will not have a torque wrench. A good rule: tighten until the rubber grommet just starts to compress, then stop. Check alignment by sitting on the bike and looking through the windscreenâit should be centred and not block your view of the front wheel. If the fairing touches the handlebars or brake lines, adjust the brackets by bending them slightly with an adjustable spanner. Test ride at low speed over bumps to listen for rattles. Re-tighten after the first 50 km.

lessons.title: Mounting Side Panels and Tank Cover
lessons.body:
Side panels and tank covers hide the battery pack and wiring, so they must fit snugly but still allow quick access for maintenance. Gather the panels, M5 bolts, nylon washers, and a 4mm Allen key. Before mounting, check that all rubber grommets and metal inserts are in placeâmissing grommets cause panels to crack. If you are missing a grommet, cut a 5mm length of fuel hose as a substitute.

Start with the tank cover. It usually slides over the top of the battery box and locks into place with two bolts at the front and two at the rear. Insert the front bolts first, then push the cover down gently until the rear holes align. Tighten to 4 Nm. Do not force the coverâif it does not sit flat, check that no wires are trapped underneath. For side panels, hook the top tab into the slot on the frame, then swing the bottom into place. Secure with one bolt at the bottom and one at the rear. Use nylon washers to protect the paint. Tighten to 4 Nm.

In dusty conditions, add a strip of foam tape along the panel edges to keep out dust and water. If the panels vibrate, stick a small piece of rubber inner tube on the inside where they touch the frame. Test the fit by pressing on each panelâthere should be no movement. Remove and refit the panels a few times to make sure you can do it quickly with the tools you carry on the bike. A common mistake is overtightening, which cracks the plastic around the bolt holes. If a hole cracks, stop-drill a 2mm hole at the end of the crack and reinforce with a washer.

lessons.title: Attaching Rear Fender and Tail Section
lessons.body:
The rear fender and tail section protect you from mud and water and also hold the rear light and number plate. You will need a 10mm spanner, a 5mm Allen key, and a drill with a 6mm bit if you need to make new holes. Start by removing the rear wheel or propping the bike so the rear is off the groundâthis gives you room to work. Check the fender for cracks, especially around the mounting points. If cracked, repair with fibreglass before installing.

Mount the rear fender to the swingarm or frame using the original bolts. Most fenders use four M6 bolts. Tighten them to 8 Nm. Make sure the fender is centred over the tyreâmeasure the gap on both sides; it should be equal. If not, adjust by loosening the bolts and shifting the fender. For the tail section, slide it over the rear frame and align the holes with the seat subframe. Bolt it at the front first, then the rear. Use blue threadlocker on these bolts because they vibrate loose. Tighten to 8 Nm.

Connect the rear light wiring before final tightening. The tail light usually has three wires: earth (black), brake (red), and tail (brown or yellow). Use a multimeter to confirm which is which. Solder and heat-shrink all connectionsâdo not use twist connectors. In Africa, rain and dust demand waterproofing. Wrap the connectors with self-amalgamating tape. Test the lights: press the brake lever, the brake light should glow brighter than the tail light. Finally, check that the number plate is visible from behind and not covered by the fender. If you carry a passenger, make sure the tail section does not rub on the tyre when the suspension compresses.

lessons.title: Securing Seat and Cushions
lessons.body:
A secure seat is critical for safety and comfort. Most EV motorbike seats are bolted to the frame with two M8 bolts at the rear and a tongue that slots under the tank cover at the front. You will need a 12mm socket, a 6mm Allen key, and a torque wrench. Start by checking the seat pan for cracks. If the pan is plastic and cracked, reinforce it with a metal plate and rivets. For cushions, if the foam is torn or compressed, replace it with high-density foam (30-40 kg/mÂ³). You can cut foam with an electric knife or a hacksaw blade.

Install the seat by sliding the front tongue under the tank cover, then lower the rear onto the mounting points. Insert the bolts and tighten to 15 Nm. Do not overtightenâyou can crush the seat pan. If the seat wobbles, add rubber washers between the seat and frame. For cushion attachment, use stainless steel staples (8mm) with a manual staple gun. Pull the cover tight and staple from the centre outwards. If you do not have staples, use contact adhesive and clamp for 24 hours.

In hot, humid climates, choose a marine-grade vinyl cover to resist mould. Add a layer of plastic sheeting between the foam and cover to stop water soaking in. Test the seat by sitting on it and bouncingâthere should be no movement. Check that the seat does not rub on the battery box or wiring. If you carry a passenger, make sure the seat is long enough and the rear cushion is secure. After 100 km, re-tighten the seat bolts.

lessons.title: Installing Foot Pegs and Guards
lessons.body:
Foot pegs and guards keep your feet secure and protect the bike in a fall. You will need a 14mm spanner, a 6mm Allen key, and a torque wrench. Start by checking the mounting brackets on the frameâthey must be straight and free of cracks. If the brackets are bent, straighten them with a hammer and anvil, or replace them. Foot pegs usually mount with a single M10 bolt and a return spring. Apply grease to the pivot pin before assembly so the peg folds smoothly.

Install the foot peg bracket to the frame using two M8 bolts. Tighten to 20 Nm. Then slide the peg into the bracket, insert the pivot pin, and secure with a split pin or circlip. Test that the peg springs back when you kick it. For passenger pegs, repeat on the rear brackets. Guardsâusually made of plastic or aluminiumâbolt to the frame or engine mounts. Use M6 bolts with rubber washers to reduce vibration. Tighten to 8 Nm. Make sure the guard does not interfere with the brake pedal or gear lever.

In Africa, foot pegs often take a beating on rough roads. Check them weekly for looseness. If the peg is worn, replace the rubber sleeve or the whole peg. For off-road use, consider wider pegs for better grip. Test ride standing on the pegsâthey should not flex. If they do, the bracket is weak; reinforce it with a gusset. Always use threadlocker on foot peg bolts. After installation, check that your boots do not slip off when wet. Clean the pegs with soap and water, not oil.

lessons.title: Final Bodywork Alignment
lessons.body:
Final alignment ensures all panels fit together with even gaps and no rattles. You will need a tape measure, a 4mm and 5mm Allen key, a 10mm spanner, and a friend to help. Start by loosening all bodywork bolts slightlyâabout half a turn. This allows the panels to shift into their natural position. Stand back and look at the bike from the front, side, and rear. Check the gaps between the fairing and tank cover, side panels and seat, and tail section and rear fender. Aim for a uniform gap of 3-5 mm.

Adjust one panel at a time. Start with the front fairing: push it up or down until the gap to the tank cover is even, then tighten its bolts to 8 Nm. Next, align the side panels so their top edges are parallel to the seat. Tighten to 4 Nm. For the tail section, make sure it is centred over the rear wheel and the gap to the seat is even. Tighten to 8 Nm. Finally, check the seatâit should sit flush with the tank cover and side panels. If not, adjust the seat mounting bolts or add shims.

Once aligned, tighten all bolts in a diagonal pattern to the specified torque. Do not overtighten. Go for a slow ride over bumps and listen for rattles. If you hear a rattle, locate it by pressing on panels while riding (have a helper do this). Common causes are missing grommets, loose bolts, or wires tapping. Fix by adding foam tape or tightening. After 100 km, re-check all bolts. In dusty conditions, alignment may shift; check monthly. A well-aligned bodywork not only looks good but also reduces vibration and extends the life of your panels.

quiz.q: What torque should you use for M6 fairing bolts?
quiz.explanation: M6 fairing bolts are typically tightened to 8 Nm to avoid cracking plastic.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean a polycarbonate windscreen?
quiz.explanation: Soapy water is safe; solvents like petrol or alcohol cloud polycarbonate.

quiz.q: What can you use as a substitute for a missing rubber grommet?
options: A) A piece of fuel hose
quiz.explanation: A 5mm length of fuel hose works as a vibration-absorbing grommet.

quiz.q: When mounting side panels, what should you use to protect the paint?
quiz.explanation: Nylon washers cushion the panel and prevent paint damage.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for tank cover bolts?
quiz.explanation: Tank cover bolts are small and should be tightened to 4 Nm.

quiz.q: What should you do if a side panel hole cracks?
options: B) Stop-drill a 2mm hole at the crack end
quiz.explanation: Stop-drilling prevents the crack from spreading.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for rear fender bolts?
quiz.explanation: Rear fender bolts are M6 and should be tightened to 8 Nm.

quiz.q: Why should you use threadlocker on tail section bolts?
options: C) To make them easier to remove
quiz.explanation: Vibration can loosen bolts; threadlocker keeps them secure.

quiz.q: How many wires does a typical rear tail light have?
quiz.explanation: Earth, brake, and tail light wires are standard.

quiz.q: What should you use to waterproof electrical connectors?
quiz.explanation: Self-amalgamating tape forms a waterproof seal.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for seat bolts?
quiz.explanation: Seat bolts are M8 and should be tightened to 15 Nm.

quiz.q: What density foam is recommended for seat cushions?
quiz.explanation: High-density foam (30-40 kg/mÂ³) provides comfort and durability.

quiz.q: What type of staple should you use for seat covers?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel staples resist rust in humid conditions.

quiz.q: What should you put between foam and seat cover to stop water soaking in?
quiz.explanation: Plastic sheeting acts as a moisture barrier.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for foot peg bracket bolts?
quiz.explanation: Foot peg brackets are M8 and should be tightened to 20 Nm.

quiz.q: What should you apply to the foot peg pivot pin before assembly?
quiz.explanation: Grease ensures smooth folding and prevents wear.

quiz.q: What should you use on foot peg bolts to prevent loosening?
quiz.explanation: Threadlocker keeps bolts tight under vibration.

quiz.q: What is the target gap for bodywork panels during final alignment?
quiz.explanation: A uniform 3-5 mm gap looks professional and allows for expansion.

quiz.q: What should you do before final tightening of all bodywork bolts?
options: B) Loosen them half a turn
quiz.explanation: Loosening allows panels to settle into natural alignment.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of bodywork rattles?
quiz.explanation: Missing grommets let panels vibrate against the frame.

quiz.q: How often should you re-check bodywork bolts in dusty conditions?
quiz.explanation: Dust and vibration can loosen bolts; monthly checks are prudent.

quiz.q: What tool can help you locate a rattle while riding?
quiz.explanation: A helper can press on panels to identify the source.

quiz.q: What should you do if a fairing mounting hole is cracked?
quiz.explanation: Fibreglass repair restores strength to cracked plastic.

quiz.q: What is the correct torque for windscreen screws?
quiz.explanation: Windscreen screws are small and should be tightened to 3 Nm.

quiz.q: What type of washer should be used with windscreen screws?
quiz.explanation: Plastic washers prevent cracking the windscreen.

quiz.q: What should you check before installing the rear fender?
quiz.explanation: Cracks can worsen and lead to failure; repair before installation.

quiz.q: How do you ensure the rear fender is centred?
options: B) Measure gap on both sides
quiz.explanation: Measuring ensures equal clearance on both sides.

quiz.q: What should you do if the seat wobbles after installation?
quiz.explanation: Rubber washers take up gaps and reduce vibration.

quiz.q: What is the recommended torque for side panel bolts?
quiz.explanation: Side panel bolts are M5 and should be tightened to 4 Nm.

quiz.q: What should you do after the first 50-100 km with new bodywork?
quiz.explanation: Vibration can loosen bolts; re-tightening ensures safety.
